title: ‘Religious’ cult of Saints: denied strictly (religion’s object is God), allowed broadly or secondarily
source_text: VIII. Si quis vero quaerat an cultus qui Sanctis impendendus est dici debeat religiosus, necne, respondent Religionem, proprie & stricte loquendo, significare virtutem specialem quae habet pro objecto cultum Dei, & quae distinguitur specie ab ea virtute qua colimus Sanctos; quae observantia quaedam est alius plane rationis: aliquando vero latius accipi Religionis nomen, videlicet, pro omni illa virtute qua colimus Deum, vel amicos Dei, aliasque res sacras, & quae distinguitur a cultu politico & mere humano. Ac priori sensu negant cultum Sanctorum esse religiosum actum, concedunt vero posteriori sensu. Sive quod eodem recidit, dicunt Sanctos coli debere cultu Religionis non primario sed secundario.
pass_a_gloss: But if anyone asks whether the cult that is to be paid to the Saints ought to be called religious, or not, they answer that Religion, properly and strictly speaking, signifies a special virtue which has for its object the cult of God, and which is distinguished in species from that virtue by which we cultivate the Saints; which is a certain observance of a plainly other reason: but sometimes the name of Religion is taken more broadly, namely, for every that virtue by which we cultivate God, or the friends of God, and other sacred things, and which is distinguished from political and merely human cult. And in the prior sense they deny that the cult of the Saints is a religious act, but they concede it in the posterior sense. Or, what comes to the same, they say the Saints ought to be cultivated with the cult of Religion not primarily but secondarily.
pass_b_english: Strictly, religion’s object is God’s cult—so saint-cult is another species of observance.
Broadly (or secondarily) they still call saint-honor religious, as opposed to mere civil polity.
